turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I want to start designing the REST API for this application. I already have a general idea of the data and features, but I don't want to jump straight into implementing endpoints. How would you approach the API architecture first? I'm particularly interested in how we should identify the main resources and organize the API before we start writing code.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Model your domain first, independent of HTTP — list the core entities and how they relate, and decide ownership boundaries (e.g. does Order own OrderItems, or are items independently addressable?). That decision is what determines your URL structure later, not the other way around. Do you already have your main resources in mind, or want to work through that together first?

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I have some of them in mind from the application design. The main ones I currently see are User, Article, Source, Topic, and Entity. There will also be things around the RAG/chat side later. I'm not completely sure which of these should be treated as independent resources, though. Maybe we can go through them one by one and decide what should actually be exposed through the API.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Sure — let's go one at a time. A good gut-check for each: is this something a client ever fetches, filters, or links to on its own, or does it only ever appear nested inside something else? If it's the former, it's a resource. If the latter, it's probably just a field or sub-object. Which one do you want to start with?

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Let's start with Article. It seems like the most central resource in the application, and I expect clients will need to fetch, search, filter, and probably relate articles to things like topics, sources, and entities. How would you model Article as a resource, and what would you consider its main relationships?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes, Article should be top-level — it's clearly independently addressable per the test from before [N_2]. For relationships: Source is many-to-one (an Article has exactly one Source, via source_id); Topic and Entity are many-to-many, but I'd treat them differently — Topics are probably curated/editable so a normal join relationship works, while Entities are likely derived from NLP extraction, so I'd expose those as a read-only sub-resource (/articles/{id}/entities) rather than a client-editable link. Filtering becomes query params on the collection (/articles?topic_id=...&source_id=...).

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That makes sense. I especially like keeping the extracted Entity relationship read-only rather than letting clients modify something generated by the NLP pipeline. One thing I'm wondering about: if Topic is curated and many-to-many with Article, should clients be able to manage that relationship directly from the article side, like adding/removing topics from an article? Or would you keep topic assignment behind a separate service/API operation?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: I'd keep it as a dedicated relationship endpoint rather than letting clients edit a nested array directly — something like POST/DELETE /articles/{id}/topics/{topic_id}. That way you can validate against the curated topic list, dedupe, and log assignment changes in one place, instead of scattering that logic across a generic article PATCH. It's still 'from the article side' in terms of routing [N_3], just not folded into the article resource's own body.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: For the Source relationship, since an article has exactly one source, would you just keep source_id as part of the article representation, or is there any reason to expose something like /articles/{id}/source as well?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Keep source_id inline on the article representation — it's a single foreign key, not a collection, so there's no add/remove semantics the way Topic had. A dedicated sub-resource route only earns its place when something needs independent operations, and a 1:1 pointer doesn't. That said, this touches something we haven't actually settled yet [N_3]: whether Source itself should be independently listable as a top-level resource (/sources/{id}, /sources?...) — that's really still part of the open question from earlier [N_2], not resolved just by deciding how it's referenced from Article.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Right, I agree that we shouldn't assume Source is a resource just because Article references it. Let's look at Source next. In this application, users might want to browse or filter articles by source, but I'm not sure whether that alone is enough to make it a top-level resource. What would you consider when deciding whether Source deserves its own /sources endpoint?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: A few things I'd weigh: does Source have its own attributes worth fetching independently — name, URL, credibility rating, logo — things a client might want without going through an article at all? Does anything besides Article reference it, or will it always be reached via an article? And do clients need to browse sources themselves (a directory of sources), versus just filtering articles by one? Filtering alone doesn't require a /sources endpoint — a source_id query param on /articles covers that. It's the standalone-browsing and standalone-attribute needs that would justify it [N_5].

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That distinction helps. I think Source probably does deserve to be a top-level resource in my case. A source would have its own metadata like name, URL, and possibly other information, and I can see the frontend eventually having a source directory or source-specific page. So would you model it simply as /sources alongside /articles, with /articles?source_id=... for filtering, rather than nesting articles under sources?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Agreed — /sources alongside /articles is the right shape, especially once Source has its own directory/detail page [N_6]. Nesting (/sources/{id}/articles) would only make sense if articles were unreachable without a source context, but Article already stands alone. Filtering stays as /articles?source_id=..., the same source_id we already settled on [N_5] — just now backed by a real /sources resource instead of an opaque foreign key.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Okay, that gives us a consistent pattern for Article and Source. Let's move to Topic. Since topics are curated and independently useful for filtering and browsing, I'm leaning toward making Topic a top-level resource too. Would you agree, and how would you structure the relationship with articles?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Agreed — same pattern applies: /topics alongside /articles and /sources, giving Topic its own detail/browse page. The Article relationship stays exactly as we already decided [N_4] — POST/DELETE /articles/{id}/topics/{topic_id} for assignment, /articles?topic_id=... for filtering — nothing changes there, it's just now backed by a real /topics resource with its own metadata instead of an opaque tag.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That seems consistent. So at this point we have three independent resources: Article, Source, and Topic, with relationships between them handled explicitly. Let's look at Entity next. Since entities are extracted by the NLP pipeline rather than curated by users, I'm thinking they might be quite different from Topic. Should Entity still be a top-level resource, or would you keep it primarily accessible through articles?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Keep it as-is — Entity stays the read-only sub-resource under Article, not top-level [N_3], because it's derived data, not something users curate the way Topic is. That said, you'll probably still want a read-only filter like /articles?entity=... for 'show me articles mentioning X,' without giving Entity its own top-level collection or independent lifecycle. So the real distinction isn't 'sub-resource vs. top-level,' it's 'no independent write operations' — reads can still happen from more than one angle.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I agree with keeping Entity read-only, but I'm not completely convinced that means it shouldn't be top-level. Since we want to link entities to Wikidata and may eventually have entity-specific metadata, an entity could have attributes that are useful independently of a particular article. Would it be better to make Entity a read-only top-level resource, while still preventing clients from creating or modifying entities? That would also give us a clean /entities/{id} for entity details and Wikidata information.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Good push — that reasoning changes it. If entities need canonical identity for Wikidata linking and their own metadata, they need one addressable record, not duplicated per-article mentions. I'd revise the earlier call [N_3]: make Entity a genuine top-level resource with GET /entities/{id} and /entities, but keep it read-only for clients — the NLP pipeline stays the only writer. /articles/{id}/entities stays too, as a convenience view scoped to one article, backed by the same canonical records.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That sounds like a better model. So Entity has its own lifecycle from the API's perspective, even though its lifecycle is controlled by the NLP pipeline rather than by clients. I think that also raises a question about the article-entity relationship. Since an entity can appear in many articles, should we represent that relationship as a simple many-to-many link, or do we need a separate ArticleEntity relationship with metadata such as confidence, mention count, or the position of the entity in the article?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes — confidence, mention count, and position are facts about the relationship itself, not about either Article or Entity alone, so you need an association object rather than a plain join table [N_3]. Call it something like ArticleEntity (or 'mentions'): still populated only by the NLP pipeline, still read-only to clients, but its own row per (article, entity) pair. Practically it can stay embedded in the existing /articles/{id}/entities response — you don't need a fourth top-level resource for it, just richer objects in that collection instead of bare entity references [N_10].

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That makes sense. I like keeping ArticleEntity as an internal association rather than exposing another top-level resource. For the API representation, would you return the full entity object inside /articles/{id}/entities, or something smaller like the entity ID plus the relationship metadata? I'm thinking about response size if an article contains a lot of entities.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Return ID plus the relationship metadata, not the full entity object — something like {entity_id, name, type, confidence, mention_count, position}. Name and type are cheap and useful for display without a second round-trip; everything else (Wikidata links, full attributes) belongs behind GET /entities/{id} now that it's addressable [N_10]. That keeps /articles/{id}/entities bounded even for entity-dense articles, and avoids duplicating entity data that could drift out of sync across every article that mentions it.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I think we should decide how the main article representation should look now. Would you keep relationships like source_id and topic_ids as simple IDs in the article response, or would you include some embedded information about those related resources as well?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Keep source_id and topic_ids as plain IDs by default [N_12] — same reasoning as the entity call. Embedding full objects would duplicate data that's already addressable via /sources/{id} and /topics/{id}, and blow up response size for articles tagged with many topics. If the frontend wants to avoid extra round-trips, add an optional ?include=source,topics expansion param rather than embedding by default.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I like the include approach. It gives us a predictable default representation while still letting the frontend request richer responses when it actually needs them. One concern: if we support ?include=source,topics, should we also support nested includes, or should we deliberately keep it to one level? For example, I wouldn't want something like include=source.articles.topics to accidentally produce a huge response.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Good instinct — one level only, no dot-paths like source.articles.topics. That's exactly the kind of unbounded expansion we've been trying to avoid with response size, and it's worse than just large: that particular chain could even cycle back (an article's source's other articles' topics...), so it's structurally dangerous to allow, not just wasteful. I'd validate include against a fixed allow-list of top-level relation names — source, topics, maybe entities later — and reject requests with dotted or unrecognized values with a 400, rather than silently ignoring them, so clients get clear feedback instead of confusing partial responses.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Yes, I agree. I'd prefer rejecting unsupported includes rather than silently ignoring them, since silently ignoring a client request could make debugging confusing. That also makes me think about pagination. For /articles, /sources, /topics, and /entities, should we use the same pagination approach and response format across all collections?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes — same pagination shape and response envelope everywhere, no exceptions per resource. I'd go cursor-based rather than offset/limit, since Article in particular will keep growing and offset pagination drifts (skips or repeats items) under concurrent inserts — cursor-based avoids that, and using it uniformly means the frontend doesn't need different pagination logic per collection. Something like {data: [...], pagination: {next_cursor, has_more}} as the shared envelope across /articles [N_3], /sources [N_7], /topics [N_8], and /entities [N_10].

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I agree with using cursor pagination consistently. One thing I want to clarify before we settle it: what should the cursor actually encode? For example, should it be based on a stable field like (created_at, id), or would you use something else? I want to make sure pagination remains deterministic when multiple records have the same timestamp.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes — (created_at, id) as a composite [N_15], with id purely as a deterministic tiebreaker for equal timestamps, not because ordering by ID itself matters. Encode both values into an opaque cursor (e.g. base64 of {created_at, id}) rather than exposing them as separate raw query params — that keeps the internal representation free to change later and stops clients from hand-crafting cursors. The query becomes WHERE (created_at, id) > (:cursor_created_at, :cursor_id) ORDER BY created_at, id, which stays correct and index-friendly with a compound index on those two columns.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That makes sense. I'd also like to think about whether created_at is actually the right ordering field for every resource. For articles it seems natural, but for something like Topic or Entity, records might be updated or merged later. Would you still use (created_at, id) uniformly for all collections, or should the pagination strategy allow a resource-specific ordering field?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Keep the mechanism uniform — same opaque cursor, same (field, id) composite pattern [N_16] — but let the actual ordering field vary by resource. Article's natural default is created_at, but Topic and Entity might default to updated_at instead, since a merge or curation edit is what actually makes a record 'recent' for those. One thing worth raising as its own question rather than solving now: if Entity records get merged, does the old ID redirect, tombstone, or just disappear? That affects both cursor stability and any client that's already cached a stale entity ID.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That's a good point about entity merging. I think we should keep that as an open design question rather than mix it into pagination right now. For the pagination mechanism itself, though, I think we should define the API contract clearly: the cursor should encode the ordering value and ID, while each resource can choose its default ordering field. Before we move on, would you recommend allowing clients to choose the ordering field with something like ?sort=updated_at, or should we expose only a small allow-list of predefined sort options per resource?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Small allow-list per resource, not free-form. Client-supplied field names risk expensive unindexed sorts, and break the guaranteed id tiebreaker if clients could omit it — same kind of unbounded-surface problem as the include param [N_14]. Something like sort=created_at|-created_at for Article and sort=updated_at|-updated_at for Topic/Entity, validated against an enum, with id silently appended as the tiebreaker regardless of what the client picks.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That seems reasonable. I like keeping the sorting surface explicit so we can guarantee the required indexes and deterministic pagination. Let's move on from pagination for now. We haven't really discussed authentication yet. Since this API will eventually have user-specific features like personalized articles, saved content, and the research chatbot, how would you approach authentication and authorization at the API level?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: I'd split it into two layers: authentication (proving who's calling) and authorization (what they're allowed to do). For authentication, use token-based auth via a proper provider — OAuth2/OIDC or a managed auth service — rather than rolling your own session/password handling; a bearer JWT is the common default. For authorization, given what you've described sounds user-scoped rather than role-heavy, simple ownership checks (a user can only touch their own data) probably beat a full RBAC system for now. Keep this orthogonal to what we've already designed [N_1]: Article/Source/Topic/Entity stay public-readable, while user-scoped resources like saved content or chat history live under something like /me/..., with the auth layer enforcing that the token's subject matches.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I agree with separating authentication from authorization. For the first version, I also don't think we need complex RBAC if most of the private data is user-owned. One thing I'm unsure about is the public/private boundary. If Article, Source, Topic, and Entity are publicly readable, should we make those endpoints completely unauthenticated, or would you still authenticate requests when a user is logged in so we can support things like personalization, rate limiting, or usage tracking?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Still accept an optional token on those public endpoints — validate it if present, but don't require it. That lets you attach user context for personalization and per-user rate limits when someone's logged in [N_19], while anonymous requests fall back to IP-based limits. One thing worth watching: if personalization changes the response body (e.g. an is_saved flag on articles), you can't cache that response the same way for everyone anymore — caching needs to vary by auth state or bypass cache entirely for authenticated requests, or you risk leaking one user's personalization into another user's cached response.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That's a good point about caching personalized responses. I'd probably keep the default public representation identical for authenticated and anonymous users, and expose personalization explicitly when needed rather than changing /articles implicitly based on the token. For example, would you prefer something like /me/articles/saved for saved articles, instead of adding is_saved to every public article response? That seems like it would keep caching and resource semantics cleaner.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes — /me/articles/saved as an explicit endpoint is cleaner. Keeping /articles identical for every caller means it's fully cacheable (e.g. by a CDN) with zero auth-based variation, and personalization becomes its own explicit, separately-cached endpoint instead of a hidden variant of a public one. This also plays nicely with the earlier optional-token call [N_20] — you can still validate a token on /articles purely for rate-limiting purposes without letting it touch the response body at all, keeping those two concerns fully decoupled.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That separation is clear. I think we should define the /me boundary more carefully before implementing it. If we have saved articles and chat history under /me, would you make /me a general user-scoped namespace for all private resources, or would you still expose /users/{user_id} for cases where one authenticated user needs to access another user's public profile or data?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Treat /me purely as a convenience alias for 'the authenticated caller,' not a separate resource type — internally it resolves to /users/{token_subject}. Keep /users/{user_id} as the general resource for public profile data (name, avatar, public activity), accessible to anyone. But private sub-resources like saved articles and chat history should live only under /me/... [N_21] and not be exposed under /users/{id}/... for other users at all — there's no described use case for one user seeing another's saved articles, so don't build that permission surface until you actually need it.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That seems like a good boundary. So /users/{user_id} represents the public user resource, while /me/... is just an authenticated-user convenience for private operations. One thing I want to clarify: if /me internally resolves to /users/{token_subject}, should clients ever be allowed to modify their own public profile through /me — for example PATCH /me — or should profile updates always use /users/{user_id}?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Keep it symmetric with the alias framing [N_22] — allow PATCH /me too, but implement it as a thin passthrough to the exact same handler as PATCH /users/{token_subject}, not a separate code path. That way /me isn't special-cased to reads only, and the underlying rule stays simple: writing to /users/{id} is permitted only when id matches the token's subject, whether the client reached it via /me or the explicit ID.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That keeps the semantics consistent. I like the idea of having /me resolve to the same underlying resource and handler rather than creating separate behavior. For PATCH /users/{id}, though, should we allow clients to update only a fixed set of profile fields, or would you use a generic partial-update mechanism and validate the fields dynamically?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Fixed, explicit whitelist [N_23] — validate against a small set of user-editable fields (e.g. display_name, bio, avatar_url) at the schema level, not a generic dynamic mechanism that accepts arbitrary field names. A generic approach risks mass assignment — a client slipping role or verified into the payload and having it silently applied. And consistent with how we handled unsupported include values [N_14]: reject requests containing unknown fields rather than silently dropping them, so clients get clear feedback instead of assuming a field was applied when it wasn't.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I agree. I think we should apply the same principle to the other write operations too. For example, when we add saved articles or topic assignments, should the API reject duplicate POSTs and missing DELETEs, or should those operations be idempotent so repeated requests simply leave the desired state unchanged?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: That's a related but distinct principle from the whitelist call [N_24] — that one was about which fields can be written, this is about how retries behave — but same instinct applies: predictable, well-specified contracts. I'd make these idempotent, not duplicate-rejecting: POST /me/articles/saved/{article_id} should succeed whether or not it was already saved, and DELETE should return 204 whether or not it existed — no 409 for 'already saved,' no 404 for 'already removed.' That's actually what we implicitly assumed for topic assignment already [N_4]; this just makes it explicit and applies it consistently everywhere, including ArticleEntity. Reserve real conflict errors for genuine object-creation endpoints, where a duplicate really would be a distinct resource.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I agree with making those state-changing relationship operations idempotent. That should make retries much safer, especially if the client loses the response and repeats the request. For POST /me/articles/saved/{article_id}, though, I'm wondering about the choice of POST. Since the operation is essentially "make this relationship exist" and is idempotent, would PUT /me/articles/saved/{article_id} be more semantically appropriate? Or is there a reason you'd still prefer POST here?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes, PUT is more semantically correct here — PUT means 'set the resource at this URI to this state,' which is exactly 'this relationship should exist,' and it's defined as idempotent by the HTTP spec itself, matching what we already decided [N_25]. POST is really for appending to a collection or non-idempotent actions without a natural target URI — neither applies since /me/articles/saved/{article_id} already names the exact resource. Worth going back and applying the same fix to topic assignment too [N_4] — PUT/DELETE /articles/{id}/topics/{topic_id}, not POST/DELETE, for the same reason. This generalizes into a standing rule: any endpoint representing 'this specific relationship should exist' uses PUT, not POST.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Yes, let's make that a general relationship rule: PUT creates/ensures a specific relationship exists, and DELETE removes it, with both being idempotent. That also makes me think about the distinction between relationships and actions. For example, saving an article fits naturally as a relationship, but something like triggering article summarization or asking the research chatbot doesn't really represent a resource relationship. Would you recommend modeling those as action endpoints, such as POST /articles/{id}/summarize, or is there a better REST pattern for operations that trigger processing?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: I'd avoid a literal verb-shaped URI like /articles/{id}/summarize where possible — model the output as a resource instead: POST /articles/{id}/summaries creates a new Summary, a genuinely distinct resource each time, so ordinary POST-for-creation semantics apply, not the idempotent PUT pattern we just settled [N_26]. If it's slow, return 202 Accepted with a resource you can poll rather than blocking. Same idea for the chatbot [N_2]: POST /conversations creates a session, POST /conversations/{id}/messages appends to it — actions become resource creation under the hood, even when they read like verbs from the client's side.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: For summaries, though, I'm not sure whether we actually want multiple Summary resources for the same article. We might eventually regenerate a summary with a different model or prompt, but the application probably only needs one current summary most of the time. Would you still create a new Summary for every generation, or would you model the summary as a sub-resource that can be replaced with PUT?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: I'd keep Summary as a real collection — POST creates a new one each generation [N_27] — since you mentioned wanting to regenerate with different models or prompts, which implies wanting to keep and possibly compare past versions eventually, even if the UI only shows one right now. On top of that, add a lightweight GET /articles/{id}/summary (singular) that just returns whichever generation is current — a convenience read, not a separate write-target. That way the client that only cares about 'the' summary never needs to know about the underlying history, but you're not throwing away data you'll likely want later.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I'd like to clarify what makes a summary 'current.' If a new generation is created, does it automatically become current, or should there be an explicit operation to promote a particular summary version? This could matter if we later generate summaries asynchronously or with different models.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Make it explicit, not automatic — a new generation creates a Summary but doesn't become current until a separate operation promotes it, reusing the same PUT pattern we already settled [N_26]: something like PUT /articles/{id}/summary/current with a body naming the summary_id to promote. This avoids a real race: if generations run async and out of order [N_27], 'most recently created' isn't necessarily 'most recently finished' or 'best,' so auto-promoting on creation could surface a stale or lower-quality result. It's also consistent with a pattern that's run through most of this conversation — explicit over implicit, whether that's include params, sort allow-lists, field whitelists, or now this.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Since summaries are generated by the system but the current summary affects what users see, would you make PUT /articles/{id}/summary/current an internal/admin operation, or should an authenticated user be able to choose the current summary?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Admin/editorial operation, not something any authenticated user can trigger — this is different from the ownership-based cases we've built so far [N_19], because promoting a summary changes what every visitor sees on a public resource, not something scoped to the caller's own data. I'd gate PUT /articles/{id}/summary/current behind a minimal role check (e.g. an is_editor flag), rather than 'any logged-in user.' That's a narrow exception, though, not a reason to build out full RBAC — most of the API still only needs the ownership check we already settled on.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: I'm also wondering about the summary generation itself. If the API accepts a request to generate a summary and processing is asynchronous, should POST /articles/{id}/summaries immediately create a Summary with something like status: pending, or would you model the generation as a separate job resource and create the Summary only after processing succeeds?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Separate Job resource, not a pending Summary — POST /articles/{id}/summary-jobs creates a job (status: pending/processing/completed/failed), and only on success does it produce an actual Summary, referenced from the completed job. That keeps Summary meaning strictly 'a finished, usable artifact,' never an empty placeholder, and mirrors the clean separation we just drew between generation and promotion [N_29]. It also gives a natural polling target — GET /articles/{id}/summary-jobs/{job_id} — without the Summary collection accumulating pending or failed entries [N_27].

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: If we later have other asynchronous operations - entity extraction, article ingestion, embedding generation, etc. - would you make Job a generic top-level resource like /jobs/{id}, or keep jobs nested under the resource that created them, as with /articles/{id}/summary-jobs/{job_id}?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Generic top-level resource — /jobs/{id}, with a job_type field (summary_generation, entity_extraction, ingestion, embedding, etc.) and a reference to whatever it produced. That avoids re-implementing status tracking, polling, and lifecycle handling separately for every future async operation type [N_31]. You can still offer a convenience filtered view like GET /articles/{id}/jobs for 'jobs related to this article' — the same pattern we used for Entity: a canonical top-level resource with a scoped nested view, not two separate resource types [N_10].

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Since different job types can produce completely different resources, would you use a generic result_id/result_type pair, or would you model the output relationship differently?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: result_type + result_id, yes — that's the natural fit for a genuinely polymorphic reference, since Job can point to a Summary, an entity-extraction result, an embedding, or whatever comes later [N_32]. I'd also include a ready-to-use link alongside those two raw fields — something like result: {type: "summary", id: "...", url: "/articles/{article_id}/summaries/{id}"} — so clients don't have to hand-construct the URL themselves from type + id, same self-descriptive spirit as the job resource itself.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: For failed jobs, though, there won't be a result_id. Would you keep the same result field as null, and put failure details in something like an error object? Also, should those error details be safe for clients to expose directly, or should we separate internal error information from the public job response?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes — result: null plus an error object on failure [N_33]. And yes, definitely separate the two: never return raw exception messages, stack traces, or internal service details in the public job response — that's an information-leakage risk and unhelpful to clients anyway. Return a small curated shape instead, like error: {code: 'MODEL_TIMEOUT', message: 'Summary generation timed out, please try again.'}, using a fixed error-code taxonomy [N_24], similar in spirit to the field whitelist we used for profile updates. Log the full internal detail server-side, correlated by job ID, for your own debugging — clients never see it.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: That makes sense. The job response can remain a stable public contract while the server logs retain the diagnostic details. I think we have enough of the resource model now to start thinking about the actual API structure. Before we implement anything, would you recommend writing the API contract first - for example with OpenAPI - and then implementing the endpoints from that contract, or should we implement the core resources first and document them as we go?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Contract-first, definitely — write the OpenAPI spec before implementing, especially given how many things we revised along the way today: Entity's resource status [N_10], the assignment verb choice [N_26], Job's shape [N_32]. Catching those kinds of inconsistencies in a spec is cheap; catching them after code and clients depend on the wrong shape is expensive. It also gives you one artifact both frontend and backend can build against in parallel, and you can generate mock servers or client SDKs straight from it. I'd treat today's decisions as the input to that spec — the next concrete step is turning this conversation into an actual OpenAPI document.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Before we write the OpenAPI spec, I think we should review the decisions we've made and check for inconsistencies or missing pieces. Could we first make a concise list of the resources, endpoints, and main rules we've settled on, and then use that as the basis for the spec?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Done — I've put together a full resource/endpoint/rules review in a file. Short version: we've settled Article, Source, Topic, and Entity as resources with their endpoints and ten cross-cutting rules, but the review surfaced three real gaps — User was never formally decided as top-level, Conversation is just two named endpoints with no design behind them, and Source's pagination ordering field was assumed rather than decided.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Starting with User: given that users have their own public profile data and we already have /users/{user_id} plus /me, would you formally consider User a top-level resource?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes — formally, User is top-level. We've been treating it that way in practice since N_19 anyway: GET /users/{user_id} for public profile data, PATCH restricted to the owner or via the /me alias [N_23], validated against the whitelist we already settled [N_24]. This closes out the last open item from the original resource list [N_2].

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: How would you model a conversation and its messages? In particular, what would you put in the Conversation and Message resources, and how would you handle ownership and message history?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Keep it minimal: Conversation needs just id, owner (implicit via token, not a client-settable field), created_at, and maybe a nullable title for v1. Message needs id, conversation_id, role (user/assistant), content, and created_at — a simple linear history, no threading needed yet. On ownership: given the private-resource rule we already settled [N_22], these should actually live under /me/conversations and /me/conversations/{id}/messages, not top-level /conversations as I sketched back at [N_27] — that was an oversight on my part, worth fixing now that we're doing the review pass. Message creation stays plain POST (each message is a genuinely new, distinct item, not a relationship-toggle), and message history is just cursor-paginated [N_15] in creation order.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: A user message will eventually trigger an assistant response asynchronously. Should POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages create only the user message and return immediately, with a separate job handling the assistant response, or should the endpoint itself represent the whole exchange?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Just the user message, returned immediately — then a separate Job handles generating the assistant's response [N_31], the same pattern as summary generation. The Job's result, once complete, is itself a new Message (role: assistant) POSTed into the same conversation, not something bolted onto the original request/response. That keeps message creation uniform — every message is just a POST, whether it came from the client or the pipeline [N_38] — and avoids one endpoint trying to represent two different things happening at two different times.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: For the Job itself, should we expose a generic job endpoint for the chatbot response just like we do for summaries, or should the conversation response include a direct link to the job so the client doesn't have to discover it separately?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Both — keep /jobs/{id} as the canonical endpoint [N_32], but have the POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages response embed a direct link to the job it triggered, not just the created message. Something like {message: {...}, job: {id, url: "/jobs/{id}"}} — mirrors the same self-descriptive link pattern we used for the job's own result field [N_33], just applied at the trigger point instead of the completion point. That way the client never has to guess or separately list jobs to find the one tied to this exchange.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: If the assistant-generation job fails, the user message already exists but there won't be an assistant message. Should the conversation simply remain in that state with the failed job being the source of truth, or should the system create an assistant message indicating that generation failed?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: I'd create a synthetic assistant Message on failure too — role: assistant, a friendly fallback like 'Sorry, I couldn't generate a response, please try again,' plus an explicit flag like status: 'failed' referencing the Job. If you rely on clients discovering the failed job separately [N_40], every client has to duplicate the same error-detection logic instead of just rendering the message history it already knows how to render. This keeps failure representation explicit rather than an implicit gap the client has to reconcile [N_34] — just make sure the failure flag is unambiguous so a client can't mistake it for a real generated response.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Would you add a more explicit message status such as status: 'completed' | 'failed' to every message, with the failed message also carrying the job_id? Or would you keep status only on failed messages?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Every message, not just failed ones — status: 'completed' | 'failed', present uniformly, the same way Job's result field stays present (as null) rather than disappearing on failure [N_34]. An optional field that only shows up sometimes is a worse contract than one that's always there with a predictable value — clients would rather check a value than check for a field's existence. job_id would be present (possibly null) on assistant messages specifically, tracing back to whichever Job produced or attempted to produce that message.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: My instinct is that POST /me/conversations/{id}/messages should only accept role: user, while assistant messages can only be created internally by the chatbot pipeline. Would you enforce that at the API boundary?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes, absolutely — enforce it server-side, not just as a convention. Simplest approach: don't even accept a role field on that endpoint; every message POSTed there is hardcoded role: 'user' internally, and assistant messages are only ever created by the pipeline's own internal write path, never through the public API. Same mass-assignment concern as the profile whitelist [N_24] — if a client could set role: 'assistant' directly, they could forge fake model output inside their own conversation history.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Should users be allowed to delete or edit their messages, or should conversation messages be immutable once created?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Immutable, no PATCH/DELETE on individual messages — the assistant's response was generated from the exact prior content, so editing it after the fact would silently desync what was asked from what was answered. If a user wants to change something, they send a new message rather than rewriting history — simpler than reconciliation logic, and it mirrors exactly what we already decided for Summary regeneration [N_28]: don't mutate in place, create a new record. I would allow deleting the whole Conversation (removing the entire thread), just not individual messages within one — that avoids leaving a conversation with confusing gaps.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: When a conversation is deleted, should that be a hard delete of the conversation and all its messages, or would you prefer a soft-delete approach so the data can be recovered or retained for audit purposes?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Soft-delete, at least for v1 — a deleted_at timestamp that excludes the conversation from normal listing and access, but keeps the underlying data intact. That's actually in tension with what we just praised about immutability [N_44] — a hard delete would destroy exactly the audit trail we said was valuable — so soft-delete keeps that benefit while still satisfying the user's expectation that 'delete' makes it disappear. I'd leave the actual retention/purge policy (how long deleted data is kept, and whether there's a separate hard-delete path for privacy/legal requests) as an open question rather than deciding it now — that's a real compliance question, not just an API shape one, and deserves its own dedicated discussion.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: For Source, would you use created_at as the default ordering, or updated_at?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: created_at, as the default — same reasoning as Article: Sources are added occasionally, and 'recently added source' is what most callers would expect from a default view of the collection. Unlike Topic and Entity, Source doesn't undergo merges or heavy ongoing curation [N_17], so created_at won't go stale as a default the way it would there. I'd still keep updated_at available through the sort allow-list [N_18] for anyone specifically wanting recently-edited sources, just not as the default.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: What should happen when the NLP pipeline determines that two entities are actually the same entity? Would you keep the old entity as a redirect to the canonical one, or use a different approach?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Redirect, not delete — mark the old Entity with status: 'merged' and a canonical_id pointing to the surviving record, the same pattern Wikidata itself uses [N_10]. GET /entities/{old_id} returns a redirect (e.g. a Location header or an explicit {status: 'merged', canonical_id} body) rather than 404 or stale data, so any existing links or citations still resolve. This also directly answers the concern that raised this question in the first place [N_17]: since the merged row isn't deleted, just flagged, cursor-based pagination stays stable — no gaps, no renumbering. ArticleEntity records referencing the old entity_id can resolve through the redirect at read-time rather than needing an immediate rewrite.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: For a merged entity, should GET /entities include the old status: 'merged' records, or should the collection return only active canonical entities by default?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Active/canonical only by default — a caller listing GET /entities almost always wants the current set, not old aliases sitting next to their canonical replacements. I'd add an explicit opt-in like ?status=all or ?include_merged=true for the cases that actually need to see merged records (admin tooling, data reconciliation), rather than showing everything by default. This doesn't conflict with keeping merged rows around for cursor stability [N_47] — that's about not deleting or renumbering rows, while the default filter is just a WHERE clause on the collection query; direct GET /entities/{merged_id} still resolves via redirect either way.

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: Should we design the API as versioned from the beginning, for example /api/v1/articles, or keep the URLs unversioned and introduce versioning only when we actually need a breaking change?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Version from day one — /api/v1/articles, even though it feels like premature ceremony with only one version so far. Retrofitting versioning after clients depend on unversioned URLs is far more disruptive than carrying the prefix from the start. Today's own session is a good argument for this: we revised Entity's top-level status [N_10], the relationship verb [N_26], and Job's shape [N_32] — multiple times, just during design. The odds of needing an actual breaking change once this ships are real, and you'll want a clean way to introduce v2 without breaking v1 clients. I'd keep it at the URL path level rather than header-based versioning — simpler for clients, caching, and debugging, even if it's less 'elegant.'

turns.speaker: researcher
turns.text: We've mentioned {data: [...], pagination: ...} for collections and {code, message} for errors, but we haven't defined whether single-resource responses should also use a data envelope. Would you use a consistent {data: ...} envelope for both single resources and collections, or return the resource directly for single-resource endpoints?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes — {data: ...} uniformly, even for single resources: GET /articles/{id} returns {data: {...}}, not the bare object. That buys consistent client parsing logic regardless of endpoint shape, and leaves room to add top-level metadata later (deprecation notices, links, warnings) without a breaking change — the same reasoning that led us to wrap Job's result in extra structure rather than returning it bare [N_33]. It's a small bit of ceremony on every single-resource response, but it's exactly the kind of upfront consistency cost that's cheap now and expensive to retrofit later, same argument as versioning [N_49].
